chicken-cuts.title: Chicken: cuts and giblets
chicken-cuts.intro: Locate four familiar portions, then distinguish two organs used in the kitchen.
chicken-cuts.scope: These are selected chicken portions, not a complete butchery diagram. Skin, bone and trimming vary by supplier.

subjects.name: Breast
subjects.summary: The broad chest portion that supplies the principal white meat of a chicken.
facts: White meat, unlike the leg portions.
subjects.distinction: A breast is not a thigh or a drumstick.
subjects.image: Pale pink boneless breast with a broad rounded end and tapered tip.

subjects.name: Thigh
subjects.summary: The dark meat portion of the upper leg, between the body and the drumstick.
subjects.distinction: The thigh is above the leg joint; the drumstick is below it.
subjects.image: Raw skin-on thigh, broad and compact, with exposed dark pink cut edge.

subjects.name: Drumstick
subjects.summary: The lower leg portion with a narrow bone end and a rounded mass of dark meat.
subjects.distinction: A drumstick is a leg cut; a drumette is part of the wing.
subjects.image: Raw skin-on lower leg, one tapered bone end and a bulbous meaty end.

subjects.name: Wing
subjects.summary: The jointed upper limb, commonly divided into a drumette, flat and tip.
subjects.distinction: The small drumette belongs to the wing, not the leg.
subjects.image: Whole raw wing bent naturally, showing drumette, two-bone flat and pointed tip.

subjects.name: Liver
subjects.summary: The soft, lobed organ that produces bile and is included among chicken giblets.
facts: Grouped with the heart and gizzard.
subjects.distinction: The liver is an organ, not a skeletal muscle cut.
subjects.image: Smooth dark reddish-brown lobed chicken liver.

subjects.name: Gizzard
subjects.summary: The thick, muscular stomach that mechanically grinds a bird's food.
facts: Grouped with the heart and liver.
subjects.distinction: Its grinding function distinguishes it from the liver.
subjects.image: Cleaned split gizzard showing two firm dark pink muscular lobes.

pork-cuts.title: Pork: six useful distinctions
pork-cuts.intro: Learn the cut before choosing the preparation: shoulder, back, belly, ribs and lower leg.
pork-cuts.scope: U.S. retail cut names are used here. Curing and smoking describe processing, not the anatomical location.

subjects.name: Boston Butt (Shoulder)
subjects.summary: A shoulder cut from the upper front of the pig, despite its misleading name.
facts: Commonly slow roasted or braised for pulled pork.
subjects.distinction: The butt is a shoulder cut, not the rear ham.
subjects.image: Thick irregular raw pork shoulder roast with visible marbling and fat seams.

subjects.name: Loin
subjects.summary: The broad back section used for pork roasts and chops.
facts: Back, between shoulder and rear leg.
Sold as a substantial roast or cut into chops.
subjects.distinction: A loin roast is larger and broader than a tenderloin.
subjects.image: Raw broad boneless pork loin roast with pale pink muscle and a fat cap.

subjects.name: Tenderloin
subjects.summary: A small, slender, tender muscle from the loin, usually sold as a long boneless piece.
subjects.distinction: Tenderloin and loin roast are different cuts and sizes.
subjects.image: Long narrow pale pink boneless pork tenderloin tapering at one end.

subjects.name: Fresh Belly
subjects.summary: The uncured underside cut with alternating layers of meat and fat.
facts: Roasting and braising are common uses.
subjects.distinction: Bacon is a cured product; fresh belly has not undergone that process.
subjects.image: Rectangular slab of uncured belly, pale skin above distinct pink and white layers.

subjects.name: Spare Ribs
subjects.summary: A rib rack from the belly side, below the loin ribs.
facts: Belly side of the rib cage.
St. Louis ribs are a trimmed form of spare ribs.
subjects.distinction: Baby back ribs come from the loin area, not this belly section.
subjects.image: Broad raw pork spare rib rack with repeated long bones and meat between them.

subjects.name: Hock
subjects.summary: A lower leg cut surrounding a joint, distinct from the foot.
facts: Available fresh, or separately cured and smoked.
subjects.distinction: A fresh hock and a smoked hock are not interchangeable product descriptions.
subjects.image: Unsmoked raw skin-on hock, compact round cut with bone visible at one end.

sources.title: Utah State Extension: pork cut chart

beef-cuts.title: Beef: where the cut begins
beef-cuts.intro: Connect six common cuts to their anatomical origins and useful kitchen distinctions.
beef-cuts.scope: These U.S. cut names describe selected portions. The corrected guide takes precedence over the original poster archive.

subjects.name: Chuck Roast
subjects.summary: A roast from the shoulder region, a familiar choice for slow-cooked beef.
facts: Pot roasting and braising suit many chuck roasts.
subjects.distinction: Chuck is a region with several muscles, not one uniform steak.
subjects.image: Raw thick chuck roast with irregular muscle seams and visible marbling.

subjects.name: Ribeye
subjects.summary: A rib-section steak recognized for generous fat marbling within the meat.
facts: Rich flavor and a tender texture.
subjects.distinction: Marbling is fat within the muscle; it differs from an outer fat cap.
subjects.image: Raw oval ribeye with central eye, curved cap muscle and fine white marbling.

subjects.name: Strip Steak
subjects.summary: A steak cut from the strip loin beside the backbone, near the tenderloin.
facts: The strip loin can be cut into steaks or kept as a roast.
subjects.distinction: Strip loin and tenderloin are neighboring but distinct muscles.
subjects.image: Raw broad oblong strip steak with a clear fat strip along one edge.

subjects.name: Tenderloin
subjects.summary: The exceptionally tender loin muscle commonly portioned into filet mignon steaks.
facts: Fine texture with comparatively little fat.
subjects.distinction: Tenderloin is not the same muscle as strip loin or ribeye.
subjects.image: Whole long raw beef tenderloin, broad at one end and tapering at the other, with fine grain and little visible fat.

subjects.name: Brisket
subjects.summary: The breast cut below the chuck and in front of the short plate.
subjects.distinction: Brisket is separate from the short plate and its diaphragm cuts.
subjects.image: Raw broad flat brisket slab with a visible thick fat layer along one side.

subjects.name: Hanger Steak
subjects.summary: A cut from the diaphragm, associated with the short plate rather than the flank.
facts: A central connective membrane separates its sections.
subjects.distinction: Hanger and flank are different cuts. The original poster placed hanger incorrectly.
subjects.image: Two long raw dark red hanger lobes with coarse lengthwise grain and central seam.

sources.title: Beef Checkoff: tenderloin steaks and broiling cuts

pacific-fish.title: Pacific: six seafood identities
pacific-fish.intro: Read body shape, fins and markings before relying on a market nickname.
pacific-fish.scope: Selected species, shown as recognition illustrations rather than identification certificates. These waters are not exclusive ranges; provenance and availability require supplier records.

subjects.name: Chinook Salmon
subjects.summary: The Pacific salmon also called king, with black spots on both lobes of the tail.
facts: Silver sides and a blue-green back.
subjects.distinction: King is another name for Chinook, not a different fish.
subjects.image: Whole silver Chinook, dark back and black spots on both tail lobes.

subjects.name: Pacific Halibut
subjects.summary: A flat, diamond-shaped fish with both eyes on its upper side.
facts: Mottled brown upper side; pale underside.
subjects.distinction: A flatfish has a very different body plan from a round fish.
subjects.image: Whole diamond-shaped halibut seen from above, both eyes on visible upper side.

subjects.name: Pacific Cod
subjects.summary: A gray-brown North Pacific fish with a conspicuous whisker-like chin barbel.
facts: Dark mottling, a pale belly and dusky fins.
subjects.distinction: The chin barbel helps distinguish it from the fish sold as black cod.
subjects.image: Whole gray-brown mottled cod with a distinct chin barbel and three dorsal fins.

subjects.name: Sablefish
subjects.summary: The North Pacific fish marketed as black cod, although it is not a member of the cod family.
subjects.distinction: A market nickname does not establish a species or family.
subjects.image: Whole dark charcoal sablefish, elongated body and no cod-like chin barbel.

subjects.name: Albacore Tuna
subjects.summary: A streamlined tuna with exceptionally long pectoral fins reaching far back along the body.
facts: Dark blue back, silver sides and a pale tail edge.
subjects.distinction: The long pectoral fins are a key feature in the NOAA profile.
subjects.image: Whole silver-blue torpedo-shaped albacore with unmistakably long pectoral fins.

subjects.name: Pacific Sardine
subjects.summary: A small schooling fish with a blue-green back and rows of dark spots along its sides.
facts: Pale flanks with dark lateral spots.
subjects.distinction: This is a named sardine species, not a label for every small canned fish.
subjects.image: Two small whole silver sardines, blue-green backs and dark flank spots.

atlantic-fish.title: Atlantic: fish and shellfish
atlantic-fish.intro: Compare four finfish with two shellfish, keeping the species names precise.
atlantic-fish.scope: Selected species, shown as recognition illustrations rather than identification certificates. These waters are not exclusive ranges; provenance and availability require supplier records.

subjects.name: Atlantic Cod
subjects.summary: A heavy-bodied North Atlantic fish with a chin barbel, mottled skin and a clear lateral line.
facts: Large head, pale belly and dark speckles.
subjects.distinction: Haddock has a distinct dark thumbprint; cod is more mottled.
subjects.image: Whole mottled olive cod with chin barbel, pale lateral line and three dorsal fins.

subjects.name: Haddock
subjects.summary: A cod-family fish bearing a conspicuous black thumbprint on each side.
subjects.distinction: The dark side patch is the memorable contrast with cod.
subjects.image: Whole silvery haddock with dark lateral line and a black patch above the pectoral fin.

subjects.name: Atlantic Mackerel
subjects.summary: A spindle-shaped fish with a blue-green back crossed by many dark wavy bars.
facts: Silver belly and a narrow, tapered body.
subjects.distinction: The wavy back markings differ from a sardine's side spots.
subjects.image: Whole slender mackerel with blue-green back, strong wavy black bars and silver belly.

subjects.name: Black Sea Bass
subjects.summary: A dark coastal fish whose dorsal fin has pale spots and bands.
facts: Black to dusky brown body with dark fins.
subjects.distinction: The full species name matters; sea bass alone covers different fish.
subjects.image: Whole dark charcoal sea bass, raised spiny dorsal fin with pale markings.

subjects.name: Atlantic Sea Scallop
subjects.summary: A two-shelled mollusk whose adductor muscle is the portion commonly served in the United States.
subjects.distinction: Sea scallop shells lack the strong ribs seen on many other scallops.
subjects.image: Relatively smooth reddish-brown scallop shell, softly fluted edge, ivory adductor meat.

subjects.name: American Lobster
subjects.summary: A large crustacean with one heavy crusher claw and one finer-edged cutting claw.
facts: Live animals are usually olive or greenish brown.
subjects.distinction: The familiar bright red color belongs to the cooked form.
subjects.image: Whole uncooked olive-brown lobster with two visibly unequal large claws.

gulf-coast-fish.title: Gulf Coast: reef, open water and shore
gulf-coast-fish.intro: Six contrasting forms introduce the range of seafood associated with Gulf Coast menus.
gulf-coast-fish.scope: Selected species, shown as recognition illustrations rather than identification certificates. These waters are not exclusive ranges; provenance and availability require supplier records.

subjects.name: Red Snapper
subjects.summary: A reddish fish with a sloping triangular face and enlarged canine teeth.
facts: Red tones vary; deeper-water fish can be redder.
subjects.distinction: Red snapper names a species, not every red-colored reef fish.
subjects.image: Whole pink-red snapper with triangular face, spiny dorsal and small canine teeth.

subjects.name: Red Grouper
subjects.summary: A robust, large-mouthed fish with a reddish-brown body and occasional pale spots.
facts: A broad head and a projecting lower jaw.
subjects.distinction: Its heavy build contrasts with the more pointed snapper profile.
subjects.image: Whole stout reddish-brown grouper, broad mouth and scattered pale side spots.

subjects.name: Mahi Mahi
subjects.summary: A brightly colored surface-water fish with a green-blue back and gold or silver lower body.
facts: Adult males have a square forehead; females are rounder.
subjects.distinction: The dolphinfish name refers to a fish, not a marine mammal.
subjects.image: Whole male mahi mahi, tall blunt forehead, long dorsal fin, green-blue and gold body.

subjects.name: Yellowfin Tuna
subjects.summary: A torpedo-shaped tuna with bright yellow dorsal and anal fins and yellow finlets.
facts: Dark blue back and yellow-to-silver underside.
subjects.distinction: Those yellow fins distinguish the pictured form from albacore.
subjects.image: Whole adult yellowfin with long yellow dorsal and anal fins and yellow finlets.

subjects.name: White Shrimp
subjects.summary: A light gray shrimp with very long antennae and a greenish tail.
subjects.distinction: White is a species name here, not a claim that the raw shell is pure white.
subjects.image: Whole translucent gray shrimp, very long antennae and subtle green tail, never cooked pink.

subjects.name: Blue Crab
subjects.summary: A swimming crab with blue claws and flattened rear legs shaped like paddles.
subjects.distinction: Its paddle-shaped rear legs are the useful visual cue.
subjects.image: Whole uncooked blue crab from above, olive shell, blue claws and rear swimming paddles.

northwest-fruits.title: Northwest fruits: orchard and bramble
northwest-fruits.intro: Contrast core fruits, a stone fruit and three very different berries.
northwest-fruits.scope: A representative study selection, not a map of native or exclusive crops. Cultivar, grower, weather, storage and imports change availability; confirm the local harvest with the supplier.

subjects.name: Apple
subjects.summary: A crisp tree fruit with seeds held in a central core.
facts: Cultivars differ in color, texture and cooking use.
subjects.distinction: A core differs from the single stone in a peach.
subjects.image: Red apple with a cut half showing the core.

subjects.name: Pear
subjects.summary: A tree fruit often shaped with a broad base and a narrower neck.
facts: Cultivars vary in shape and color.
subjects.distinction: Pears have a seed core, not a single stone.
subjects.image: Green-gold pear with a cut half showing its core.

subjects.name: Sweet Cherry
subjects.summary: A small, fleshy tree fruit surrounding one hard stone, often eaten fresh.
facts: Cultivars can be yellow or red.
subjects.distinction: Sweet and tart cherries are distinct culinary categories.
subjects.image: Deep red sweet cherries on slender stems, one cut to show its stone.

subjects.name: Blueberry
subjects.summary: A small blue berry bearing a crown-shaped calyx at its tip.
subjects.distinction: Blueberries are not miniature grapes.
subjects.image: Blue berries with powdery bloom and clearly visible five-point crowns.

subjects.name: Raspberry
subjects.summary: A cluster of small drupelets that leaves its core behind when picked.
subjects.distinction: Blackberries retain their core.
subjects.image: Red raspberries, one turned to reveal the hollow center.

subjects.name: Blackberry
subjects.summary: A dark bramble fruit made of drupelets around a core that remains inside when picked.
facts: The core stays with the fruit.
subjects.distinction: A black raspberry is hollow; a blackberry is not.
subjects.image: Glossy black-purple blackberries with large drupelets and a cut fruit showing the core.

sources.title: University of Maryland Extension: fruit groups

northwest-vegetables.title: Northwest vegetables: from shoot to squash
northwest-vegetables.intro: Identify six plant parts: shoots, roots, buds, bulbs and mature fruit.
northwest-vegetables.scope: A representative study selection, not a map of native or exclusive crops. Cultivar, grower, weather, storage and imports change availability; confirm the local harvest with the supplier.

subjects.name: Asparagus
subjects.summary: Tender young shoots harvested as pointed spears.
subjects.distinction: The spear is a shoot, not a root.
subjects.image: A short bundle of green asparagus spears with tightly closed purple-green tips.

subjects.name: Beet
subjects.summary: A swollen, usually rounded root crop with edible leafy tops.
facts: Cultivars include red and golden forms.
subjects.distinction: The root and the greens offer different textures.
subjects.image: Deep red beet with stems and leaves, one cut face.

subjects.name: Broccoli
subjects.summary: A branching green head made of tightly packed, unopened flower buds.
facts: The head is harvested before flowers open.
subjects.distinction: The head is not a compact ball of leaves like cabbage.
subjects.image: Green broccoli crown with branching pale-green stalk and fine bud texture.

subjects.name: Carrot
subjects.summary: A fleshy, tapered taproot, commonly orange.
subjects.distinction: A carrot is a root, unlike a potato stem tuber.
subjects.image: Orange carrots with slender tips and feathery green tops.

subjects.name: Onion
subjects.summary: An edible bulb with layers beneath a dry outer skin.
facts: Bulbs and tops can be used raw or cooked.
subjects.distinction: A bulb differs from a solid root or stem tuber.
subjects.image: Golden-brown onion and a cut half showing concentric layers.

subjects.name: Winter Squash (Butternut)
subjects.summary: A mature, hard-rinded squash with a long neck and a rounded seed cavity.
facts: Orange flesh within a tan rind.
subjects.distinction: Winter squash is harvested mature; summer squash is picked young.
subjects.image: Tan butternut squash with orange cut half and seeds only in the bulbous end.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: vegetable harvest stages

southwest-fruits.title: Southwest fruits: cactus, palm and orchard
southwest-fruits.intro: Look inside each fruit to distinguish its seeds, segments, flesh and rind.
southwest-fruits.scope: A representative study selection, not a map of native or exclusive crops. Cultivar, grower, weather, storage and imports change availability; confirm the local harvest with the supplier.

subjects.name: Prickly Pear
subjects.summary: The fleshy fruit of an Opuntia cactus, distinct from its flattened green pads.
facts: Fruit color varies with species and cultivar.
subjects.distinction: The fruit and the pad are different parts of the cactus.
subjects.image: Magenta-red oval cactus fruits, one opened to show small seeds, a small pad behind.

subjects.name: Pomegranate
subjects.summary: A round, leathery fruit containing many juicy seed coverings inside pale partitions.
facts: The juice has a sweet-tart character.
subjects.distinction: The juicy interior differs from the thick outer rind.
subjects.image: Deep red pomegranate cut open to reveal ruby arils and pale membranes.

subjects.name: Date
subjects.summary: A sweet, oblong palm fruit with one elongated seed.
facts: Commercial dates come from Phoenix dactylifera.
subjects.distinction: Date palm fruit is not a dried plum.
subjects.image: Amber-brown wrinkled dates, one split to show its long seed.

subjects.name: Orange
subjects.summary: A citrus fruit with a peel surrounding juicy segments.
facts: Sweet orange is a citrus hybrid.
subjects.distinction: Its segments differ from the seed-filled cavity of a melon.
subjects.image: Whole bright orange and a half showing radial juicy segments.

subjects.name: Fig
subjects.summary: A soft fruiting structure with tiny flowers and fruits enclosed inside.
subjects.distinction: The flowers develop inside, not as an obvious outer blossom.
subjects.image: Purple fig with a cut half exposing a pink seedy interior.

subjects.name: Watermelon
subjects.summary: A large, juicy vine fruit with a substantial rind.
facts: Flesh can be red, pink or yellow.
subjects.distinction: Seeded and seedless cultivars both exist.
subjects.image: Green striped melon and red wedge with black seeds and pale rind.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: true date palm
FAO: date fruit and seed structure

southwest-vegetables.title: Southwest vegetables: peppers and garden fruits
southwest-vegetables.intro: Separate flavor, shape and harvest stage without assuming a fixed heat or season.
southwest-vegetables.scope: A representative study selection, not a map of native or exclusive crops. Cultivar, grower, weather, storage and imports change availability; confirm the local harvest with the supplier.

subjects.name: Chile Pepper
subjects.summary: An elongated Capsicum fruit used for varying degrees of heat.
facts: Heat varies by cultivar and growing conditions.
subjects.distinction: The pictured Anaheim-style form does not promise a fixed heat level.
subjects.image: Long smooth green Anaheim-style chile with a tapered point.

subjects.name: Tomatillo
subjects.summary: A small, tart, tomato-like fruit enclosed by a papery husk.
subjects.distinction: It is not simply an unripe tomato.
subjects.image: Round green tomatillos with dry papery husks peeled back.

subjects.name: Sweet Corn
subjects.summary: Tender kernels arranged in rows on an ear, harvested while still juicy.
facts: Kernels at harvest release milky juice.
subjects.distinction: Sweet corn is harvested before dry grain corn.
subjects.image: Yellow sweet corn ear with rows of kernels and green husk peeled back.

subjects.name: Zucchini
subjects.summary: An elongated summer squash picked while its skin and seeds are tender.
facts: Green, gray and golden forms exist.
subjects.distinction: It is a summer squash, even when used in a warm cooked dish.
subjects.image: Long smooth dark green zucchini with pale cut round and tiny seeds.

subjects.name: Bell Pepper
subjects.summary: A blocky, sweet pepper with thick walls and a hollow seed cavity.
facts: Mature fruit colors vary by cultivar.
subjects.distinction: Bell peppers lack the pungency of hot chile types.
subjects.image: Glossy red blocky bell pepper and half showing hollow ribs and pale seeds.

subjects.name: Winter Squash (Butternut)
subjects.summary: A mature, hard-rinded squash with a long neck and a rounded seed cavity.
facts: Orange flesh within a tan rind.
subjects.distinction: Winter squash is harvested mature; summer squash is picked young.
subjects.image: Tan butternut squash with orange cut half and seeds only in the bulbous end.

midwest-fruits.title: Midwest fruits: six market forms
midwest-fruits.intro: Compare pome, stone, berry, grape and melon forms familiar to the fruit stand.
midwest-fruits.scope: A representative study selection, not a map of native or exclusive crops. Cultivar, grower, weather, storage and imports change availability; confirm the local harvest with the supplier.

subjects.name: Apple
subjects.summary: A crisp tree fruit with seeds held in a central core.
facts: Cultivars differ in color, texture and cooking use.
subjects.distinction: A core differs from the single stone in a peach.
subjects.image: Red apple with a cut half showing the core.

subjects.name: Tart Cherry
subjects.summary: A sour red stone fruit commonly used in cherry pies.
subjects.distinction: It differs from the sweet cherry often served fresh.
subjects.image: Small bright red tart cherries, one cut to show its central stone.

subjects.name: Strawberry
subjects.summary: A red fruit with small seed-like achenes on its outer surface.
subjects.distinction: Those outer dots are tiny fruits, each containing a seed.
subjects.image: Red strawberry with green calyx and visible surface achenes.

subjects.name: Blueberry
subjects.summary: A small blue berry bearing a crown-shaped calyx at its tip.
subjects.distinction: Blueberries are not miniature grapes.
subjects.image: Blue berries with powdery bloom and clearly visible five-point crowns.

subjects.name: Grape (Concord)
subjects.summary: A dark purple, seeded grape commonly used for juice and jelly.
facts: Fruit borne in bunches on a vine.
subjects.distinction: Concord and muscadine are different grape types.
subjects.image: Loose bunch of round purple Concord grapes with a dusty bloom.

subjects.name: Cantaloupe
subjects.summary: An orange-fleshed muskmelon with a netted rind and a central seed cavity.
facts: A netted rind surrounds a central seed cavity.
subjects.distinction: Cantaloupe and watermelon are different melon crops.
subjects.image: Tan netted round melon with a cut orange-fleshed wedge and central seeds.

midwest-vegetables.intro: Read the differences between kernels, fruit, tuber, pod, leaf and squash.
midwest-vegetables.scope: A representative study selection, not a map of native or exclusive crops. Cultivar, grower, weather, storage and imports change availability; confirm the local harvest with the supplier.

subjects.name: Sweet Corn

subjects.image: Yellow sweet corn ear with rows of kernels and green husk peeled back.

subjects.name: Tomato
subjects.summary: A fleshy, seed-bearing fruit used as a vegetable in the kitchen.
facts: Cultivars vary greatly in size and color.
subjects.distinction: Botanical fruit and culinary vegetable describe different things.
subjects.image: Ripe red tomato with green calyx and cut half showing seed chambers.

subjects.name: Potato
subjects.summary: An underground stem tuber with buds called eyes.
subjects.distinction: A sweet potato is a storage root, not this kind of tuber.
subjects.image: Brown-skinned potatoes, shallow eyes visible, one cut to show pale flesh.

subjects.name: Green Bean
subjects.summary: A common bean harvested as a tender pod before its seeds become prominent.
facts: Green, yellow and purple pod types exist.
subjects.distinction: Snap beans differ from beans grown for mature dry seeds.
subjects.image: Slender green bean pods with one opened to show small immature seeds.

subjects.name: Cabbage
subjects.summary: A compact head made of leaves wrapped tightly around one another.
facts: Heads can be round, flattened or pointed.
subjects.distinction: The head is leafy, unlike broccoli's flower buds.
subjects.image: Round green cabbage with overlapping leaves and a cut wedge.

northeastern-vegetables.intro: A compact lesson in the edible parts beneath familiar market names.
northeastern-vegetables.scope: A representative study selection, not a map of native or exclusive crops. Cultivar, grower, weather, storage and imports change availability; confirm the local harvest with the supplier.

subjects.name: Asparagus
subjects.summary: Tender young shoots harvested as pointed spears.
subjects.distinction: The spear is a shoot, not a root.
subjects.image: A short bundle of green asparagus spears with tightly closed purple-green tips.

subjects.name: Pea (Garden)
subjects.summary: A shelling pea whose round seeds are removed from the pod.
facts: Also called English or shelling pea.
subjects.distinction: Snow and snap peas are selected for edible pods.
subjects.image: Open bright green garden pea pod holding round peas.

subjects.name: Beet
subjects.summary: A swollen, usually rounded root crop with edible leafy tops.
facts: Cultivars include red and golden forms.
subjects.distinction: The root and the greens offer different textures.
subjects.image: Deep red beet with stems and leaves, one cut face.

subjects.name: Carrot
subjects.summary: A fleshy, tapered taproot, commonly orange.
subjects.distinction: A carrot is a root, unlike a potato stem tuber.
subjects.image: Orange carrots with slender tips and feathery green tops.

subjects.name: Potato
subjects.summary: An underground stem tuber with buds called eyes.
subjects.distinction: A sweet potato is a storage root, not this kind of tuber.
subjects.image: Brown-skinned potatoes, shallow eyes visible, one cut to show pale flesh.

subjects.name: Winter Squash (Butternut)
subjects.summary: A mature, hard-rinded squash with a long neck and a rounded seed cavity.
facts: Orange flesh within a tan rind.
subjects.distinction: Winter squash is harvested mature; summer squash is picked young.
subjects.image: Tan butternut squash with orange cut half and seeds only in the bulbous end.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: vegetable harvest stages

southeastern-fruits.title: Southeast fruits: from peach to muscadine
southeastern-fruits.intro: Explore contrasting fruit forms, including the thick-skinned muscadine.
southeastern-fruits.scope: A representative study selection, not a map of native or exclusive crops. Cultivar, grower, weather, storage and imports change availability; confirm the local harvest with the supplier.

subjects.name: Peach
subjects.summary: A fuzzy-skinned stone fruit with flesh surrounding a single hard pit.
facts: Peaches and nectarines belong to the same species.
subjects.distinction: Nectarines have smooth skin; peaches are fuzzy.
subjects.image: Golden-red fuzzy peach with a cut half showing its stone.

subjects.name: Orange
subjects.summary: A citrus fruit with a peel surrounding juicy segments.
facts: Sweet orange is a citrus hybrid.
subjects.distinction: Its segments differ from the seed-filled cavity of a melon.
subjects.image: Whole bright orange and a half showing radial juicy segments.

subjects.name: Strawberry
subjects.summary: A red fruit with small seed-like achenes on its outer surface.
subjects.distinction: Those outer dots are tiny fruits, each containing a seed.
subjects.image: Red strawberry with green calyx and visible surface achenes.

subjects.name: Blueberry
subjects.summary: A small blue berry bearing a crown-shaped calyx at its tip.
subjects.distinction: Blueberries are not miniature grapes.
subjects.image: Blue berries with powdery bloom and clearly visible five-point crowns.

subjects.name: Watermelon
subjects.summary: A large, juicy vine fruit with a substantial rind.
facts: Flesh can be red, pink or yellow.
subjects.distinction: Seeded and seedless cultivars both exist.
subjects.image: Green striped melon and red wedge with black seeds and pale rind.

subjects.name: Muscadine Grape
subjects.summary: A large, thick-skinned grape that grows singly or in small groups.
facts: Fruit of a southern U.S. native vine.
Cultivars may be bronze or purple-black.
subjects.distinction: Its loose grouping differs from a dense Concord bunch.
subjects.image: Several large bronze and purple-black muscadines in a small loose cluster.

southeastern-vegetables.title: Southeast vegetables: leaves, pods and roots
southeastern-vegetables.intro: Learn the edible part behind six familiar Southern ingredients.
southeastern-vegetables.scope: A representative study selection, not a map of native or exclusive crops. Cultivar, grower, weather, storage and imports change availability; confirm the local harvest with the supplier.

subjects.name: Okra
subjects.summary: A ridged, edible seed pod that can thicken dishes through its mucilage.
facts: A warm-season member of the mallow family.
subjects.distinction: The pod is a fruiting structure, not a root.
subjects.image: Slender green ridged okra pods and star-shaped cut rounds.

subjects.name: Collard Greens
subjects.summary: Large, broad brassica leaves grown without forming a tight cabbage head.
subjects.distinction: Collards remain open-leaved rather than heading like cabbage.
subjects.image: Bundle of large deep green collard leaves with thick pale central veins.

subjects.name: Sweet Potato
subjects.summary: A thickened storage root, often shown with orange flesh.
facts: Flesh and skin colors vary by cultivar.
subjects.distinction: It differs botanically from both potato and true yam.
subjects.image: Copper-skinned sweet potatoes with an orange cut face.

subjects.name: Southern Pea (Black-eyed)
subjects.summary: A cowpea with pale seeds marked by a dark eye.
subjects.distinction: Cowpeas differ from cool-season garden peas.
subjects.image: Cream-colored black-eyed peas beside an opened long tan pod.

subjects.name: Summer Squash (Crookneck)
subjects.summary: A yellow squash with a curved neck, picked before the rind hardens.
subjects.distinction: Summer and winter squash describe harvest and use, not just calendar dates.
subjects.image: Yellow crookneck squash, slender bent neck and bulbous base.

subjects.name: Peanut
subjects.summary: A legume whose seed-filled pods develop underground.
facts: The familiar shell is the pod.
subjects.distinction: Despite the name, it is not a tree nut.
subjects.image: Tan textured peanut pods with one opened to reveal two reddish-skinned seeds.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: Southern Pea (Black-eyed)
University of Maryland Extension: Summer Squash (Crookneck)

culinary-spices.title: Spices: from fruit to flower
culinary-spices.intro: Whole ingredients reveal a spice's origin before it becomes a powder.
culinary-spices.scope: These six single ingredients are not blends. The cinnamon drawing represents the general bark form, not a certified species.

subjects.name: Black Pepper
subjects.summary: Small peppercorns made from the fruit of the tropical vine Piper nigrum.
subjects.distinction: Black, white and green peppercorns come from the same species but differ in harvest and processing.
subjects.image: Small dark wrinkled peppercorns in a neat loose pile.

subjects.name: Cumin
subjects.summary: Slender, tan, ridged spice fruits used as a whole or ground seasoning.
subjects.distinction: Cumin is not coriander; their shapes and aromas differ.
subjects.image: Slender tan-brown cumin seeds with clear lengthwise ridges.

subjects.name: Coriander
subjects.summary: The round, tan seed spice from the same plant whose leaves are called cilantro.
subjects.distinction: Cilantro leaves and coriander spice are different parts of one plant.
subjects.image: Round pale tan coriander seeds with delicate ridged surfaces.

subjects.name: Cinnamon
subjects.summary: An aromatic spice made from tree bark, sold as rolled quills or powder.
facts: Several Cinnamomum species supply cinnamon spices.
subjects.distinction: A cinnamon quill is rolled bark, not a hollow stem.
subjects.image: Brown rolled cinnamon bark sticks with visible curled cut ends.

subjects.name: Turmeric
subjects.summary: A yellow-orange spice obtained from the underground rhizomes of Curcuma longa.
facts: Fresh rhizome or processed ground spice.
subjects.distinction: Its rhizome is different from a seed or a true root.
subjects.image: Knobbly tan turmeric rhizomes, one cut open to show vivid orange flesh.

subjects.name: Cloves
subjects.summary: Dried, unopened flower buds with a small rounded head and a narrow stalk-like base.
subjects.distinction: A clove spice bud is unrelated to a clove of garlic.
subjects.image: Dark brown nail-shaped cloves with intact rounded bud heads.

sources.title: Kew: the plants behind Christmas spices
Herb Society of America: cumin fruits and ridges

culinary-mushrooms.title: Mushrooms: six cultivated market forms
culinary-mushrooms.intro: Compare cap, gill and cluster shapes, including three forms of one familiar species.
culinary-mushrooms.scope: This is a guide to purchased culinary mushrooms, not a wild-foraging identification guide. The first three subjects intentionally share a species.

subjects.name: White Button
subjects.summary: A small, white-capped cultivated form of Agaricus bisporus.
subjects.distinction: White button, cremini and portobello belong to the same species; cap color alone is not an age clock.
subjects.image: Small closed white button mushrooms with smooth rounded caps.

subjects.name: Cremini
subjects.summary: A small brown-capped cultivated form also known as baby bella.
subjects.distinction: Cremini and portobello are brown forms of the same species.
subjects.image: Small closed chestnut-brown cremini caps with short pale stems.

subjects.name: Portobello
subjects.summary: The broad, open-capped form of Agaricus bisporus, with prominent dark gills.
facts: Often grilled or cooked as a whole cap.
subjects.distinction: Portabella is an alternative spelling, not another species.
subjects.image: Large open brown cap with underside tilted to show dark radiating gills.

subjects.name: Shiitake
subjects.summary: An umbrella-capped mushroom with tan gills and a stem that can be fibrous.
subjects.distinction: A tough stem can be removed and used to flavor stock.
subjects.image: Brown umbrella cap with pale gills and a curved slender stem.

subjects.name: Oyster
subjects.summary: A cultivated mushroom sold in clusters of overlapping, fan-shaped caps.
facts: Clusters can be cooked whole or separated.
subjects.distinction: The seafood name refers to its form; it is a fungus.
subjects.image: Cluster of pale gray oyster fans with gills running toward their joined stems.

subjects.name: Maitake
subjects.summary: A clustered mushroom with many rippling, feather-like fronds, also called hen of the woods.
subjects.distinction: Its frilled cluster differs from a single large portobello cap.
subjects.image: Dense gray-brown maitake cluster composed of many small rippling fans.

sources.title: Penn State Extension: white and brown Agaricus strains

great-cheeses.title: Cheese: milk, make and maturation
great-cheeses.intro: Read a cheese through its milk, texture and method before relying on color.
great-cheeses.scope: The illustration shows representative forms. Producer, age and handling affect texture and flavor; protected names identify particular products.

subjects.name: Parmigiano Reggiano
subjects.summary: A hard, matured cheese with a granular structure that breaks into irregular pieces.
facts: Texture becomes more granular with age.
subjects.distinction: Its pale interior may contain small crystals; they are not blue mold.
subjects.image: Pale straw hard cheese wedge with rough fractured face, small crystals and dark rind.

subjects.name: Cheddar
subjects.summary: A firm cheese available in white and colored forms and a range of maturities.
subjects.distinction: An orange color does not by itself indicate greater age or stronger flavor.
subjects.image: Solid firm Cheddar wedge with a dense face, no large holes or blue veins.

subjects.name: Brie
subjects.summary: A soft cheese with a white surface rind surrounding a creamy interior.
facts: The interior softens as the cheese ripens.
subjects.distinction: The white outer rind differs from blue veins inside a cheese.
subjects.image: Round white-rinded Brie with a cut wedge exposing a smooth creamy interior.

subjects.name: Roquefort
subjects.summary: A sheep's milk cheese with blue-green veins in an ivory interior.
facts: Penicillium roqueforti develops within the cheese.
subjects.distinction: Roquefort is not an orange-colored blue cheese.
subjects.image: Moist ivory wedge with irregular blue-green veins, never orange paste.

subjects.name: Mozzarella di Bufala Campana
subjects.summary: A fresh stretched-curd cheese made with buffalo milk.
subjects.distinction: Mozzarella can also be made with cow's milk; this full name identifies the buffalo product.
subjects.image: Smooth porcelain-white mozzarella ball with a cut piece revealing moist layered curd.

subjects.name: Comté
subjects.summary: A matured raw cow's milk cheese from the Jura, made with a cooked and pressed curd.
subjects.distinction: Cooked curd describes cheesemaking, not a ready-made hot cheese dish.
subjects.image: Pale straw Comté wedge with natural brown rind and a mostly closed interior.

sources.title: Mozzarella di Bufala Campana Consortium: production
Parmigiano Reggiano Consortium: ingredients and maturation

charcuterie.title: Charcuterie: cut and process
charcuterie.intro: Distinguish whole muscle from sausage, pork from beef, and curing from cooking.
charcuterie.scope: These are finished product identities, not home-curing instructions. Ingredient and process details can vary; use the producer's specification for the product served.

subjects.name: Prosciutto di Parma
subjects.summary: A dry-cured whole-muscle ham made from the rear leg of the pig.
subjects.distinction: Prosciutto di Parma is a cured ham, not a cooked ham or a ground sausage.
subjects.image: Rose-pink translucent ham slices with a white fat edge beside a cured ham piece.

subjects.name: Pancetta
subjects.summary: Cured pork belly, often presented as a slab or rolled into a cylinder.
subjects.distinction: Its belly origin distinguishes it from cheek-based guanciale.
subjects.image: Rolled pancetta with a cut spiral of pink meat and white fat.

subjects.name: Guanciale
subjects.summary: A cured pork cheek or jowl cut with a substantial proportion of fat.
subjects.distinction: The anatomical cut differs from pancetta even when both are used for their fat.
subjects.image: Thick triangular cured jowl with broad ivory fat and a narrow pink meat band.

subjects.name: Salame Milano
subjects.summary: A cured sausage recognized by its fine, rice-grain-like distribution of meat and fat.
subjects.distinction: The small fat particles differ from mortadella's larger white cubes.
subjects.image: Cylindrical red salami with a sliced face densely speckled with tiny white fat pieces.

subjects.name: Mortadella Bologna
subjects.summary: A cooked, finely ground pork sausage containing distinct cubes of pork fat.
facts: Pink interior with visible white fat cubes.
subjects.distinction: Charcuterie includes cooked products as well as dry-cured ones.
subjects.image: Large smooth pink sausage cross-section with evenly spaced white fat cubes.

subjects.name: Bresaola della Valtellina
subjects.summary: A cured whole-muscle beef product made from selected hindquarter cuts.
subjects.distinction: It differs from the pork products elsewhere on this board.
subjects.image: Lean deep red cured beef slices with minimal fat beside a dark exterior piece.
